newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Iran scores initial victory in case against U.S..
newsitem.headline: Iran scores initial victory in case against U.S..

text.p: Iran scored an initial victory in a legal battle with the United States on Thursday when the International Court of Justice ruled it could hear a dispute over the destruction of Iranian oil platforms by U.S. warships.
The U.N. court's decision was a setback for Washington which had argued that Iran could not found its case on the basis of the 1955 Treaty of Amity between the two countries.
Iran claims the destruction of the three oil platforms in October 1987 and April 1988 violated international law and Washington should be ordered to pay damages.
The United States contends its actions were legitimate military retaliation because the platforms had been used to launch attacks on U.S. warships and neutral merchant ships.
The dispute relates to the final stages of the 1980-88 war between Iran and Iraq when the United States sent naval forces to the Gulf to protect international shipping.
The court's ruling that it has jurisdiction over the case clears the way for further proceedings on the issues at the heart of the dispute.
These are likely to take several years and the United States gas already indicated that it might file a countersuit against Iran for damage caused to U.S. vessels at the time.
Court president Mohammed Bedjaoui said the 16 judges voted 14 to two to reject the U.S. objection to the Treaty of Amity as a basis for jurisdiction and to hear Iran's claims.
U.S. lawyers had argued that political and military matters fell outside the scope of the treaty.
The head of Iran's delegation, Mohammed Zahedin Labaff, said he was delighted with the court's decision. "It is a rightful and just decision and a fair reading of the Treaty of Amity," he said.

U.S. State Department lawyer Michael Matheson said the court's ruling "in no way suggests that it agreed with Iran on the merits of the case. We shall defend this vigorously on the merits and continue to deny U.S. actions were unlawful."
Washington had agreed towards the end of the Iran-Iraq war to reregister Kuwaiti oil tankers under its flag so they would enjoy U.S. navy protection.
Iran viewed Kuwait as an enemy at the time because it aided Iraq financially and let in arms for Iraq through its ports.

In October 1987, U.S. warships bombarded an offshore Iranian oil platform which Washington said was being used as a base for Iranian gunboats. It acted after an Iranian Silkworm missile hit a re-flagged oil tanker in Kuwaiti waters, injuring 18 crewmen.
In April 1988, U.S. forces destroyed two more Iranian platforms after the U.S. frigate Samuel B. Roberts struck a mine, allegedly laid by Iran, in international waters.
The International Court of Justice, based in The Hague, is the judicial arm of the United Nations and settles disputes between states in accordance with international law.
Before it can hear a case, the court has to be satisfied that the states in question have recognised its jurisdiction.
